posts.heading: September 13, 2026
posts.text:
The final hours confirmed the station’s exceptional activity level, with one hundred forty-two total visits far outpacing the recent daily average of fifty. While the afternoon log highlighted the steady presence of Tufted Titmice, the evening brought a noticeable increase in American Crows, with ten detections recorded in the eighteen-hundred hour alone.

The last visual contact before dusk was a Tufted Titmouse, observed at seventeen twenty-nine just over an hour before sunset. This closed out a day where the bird remained the dominant visual subject, accounting for seventy confident sightings from the pre-dawn start to the evening wind-down. The auditory track continued to be led by Northern Cardinals and Blue Jays, which maintained high detection counts through the final hour.

As the light faded, the station settled into its nightly quiet, having logged fifteen distinct species.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 88 feeder visits and eleven species, marking a significantly busier day than the recent average of forty-three visits. Tufted Titmice dominated the visual record with forty-nine visits, while the auditory track was led by Eastern Towhees and American Crows. This level of activity exceeds the previous week’s quieter days, such as the twenty-three visits recorded on Wednesday, though it remains comparable to the peak traffic seen on Thursday and Friday.

Mourning Dove was heard for the first time at this station. The male Northern Cardinal continued to visit the ground bowl installed earlier this week, joining a list of regulars that includes Carolina Wrens and Blue Jays. Species like the Red-shouldered Hawk and Northern Mockingbird, present earlier in the week, were absent from today’s log.

The day’s high volume aligns with the steady flow of visitors since the feeders were installed and refilled earlier this week. Tufted Titmice remained the primary feeder users, while Carolina Chickadees and Mourning Doves provided consistent secondary traffic. The station’s activity has stabilized at this higher level compared to the sparse recordings from the beginning of the week.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 103 feeder visits and 12 species, marking a significant jump from the past week's average of 28 visits. Carolina Wrens and Tufted Titmice remained the dominant regulars, with the Wren's persistent chorus bridging the day from early morning to dusk. This level of activity contrasts with the quieter start to the week, though it follows the busy days of September 9 and 10.

A first confident visual record of an American Goldfinch was seen alongside the usual brown and gray regulars. The American Crow was the last visual record of the day, observed near the water bowl that was installed earlier in the week. Other species, including Red-shouldered Hawks and Northern Mockingbirds, were absent from today's count.

The presence of the hummingbird and the increased crow activity align with the new nectar feeder and treat bowl installed on September 7 and 10. These station changes provided new food sources utilized throughout the past few days.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded a significant increase in activity compared to the quiet start of the week, with thirteen species and ninety feeder visits far exceeding the recent daily averages. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees maintained a steady presence on the feeders, while the auditory record was dominated by the Carolina Wren and American Crow. This surge aligns with the installation of the nectar and seed feeders on September 7.

Morning highlights included the first confident visual records of Mourning Doves and White-breasted Nuthatches at this station. The Tufted Titmouse arrived before sunrise, and a Northern Mockingbird provided the final visual contact in the late afternoon.

The day ended with a dense vocal landscape, as two hundred and twenty-one detections surpassed the recent average of one hundred and seven. The station remains active with the new feeders and bowls installed over the past few days.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The station closed with its busiest activity in the past week, recording 23 feeder visits and 11 species, a sharp contrast to the five preceding days which averaged zero visual sightings. The high count aligns with the installation of a nectar feeder and a tube seed feeder on September 7. These three species, along with the Carolina Chickadee and Blue Jay, were not recorded during the previous week, marking a significant expansion in the visual log.

The Ruby-throated Hummingbird made the first confident visual appearance of the day, appearing 274 minutes after sunrise. By the end of the day, the Northern Mockingbird provided the last clear sighting, perched on a wire 20 minutes before sunset.

The Blue Jay and Red-bellied Woodpecker led the late-day detections, adding to the day's total of 238 vocal records. This surge in both visual and audio data stands out against the recent quiet period, where detection averages hovered around 42.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
Yesterday’s 79 detections stood in sharp contrast to the five recorded on Monday, with the six species detected marking a significant jump from the single day of activity earlier this week. While the station remained visually silent with no feeder visits, the auditory log captured a full day of sound, led by Red-bellied Woodpeckers and Carolina Wrens.

The activity spread across the day rather than clustering in a single burst, a departure from the brief vocalizations recorded on Monday. Red-shouldered Hawks were heard in the late morning, adding to the roster of species recorded on this site for the first time.

New feeders installed on the pole on Monday were not visited during the day, keeping the physical log empty despite the high volume of calls. The day’s total reflects a sustained presence of sound, with Eastern Towhees and Blue Jays contributing to the final counts as the light faded.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged its first day of data, recording five audio detections and no visual contacts. This marks the first recorded activity for the Carolina Wren and the Eastern Towhee at this location.

Two feeders were installed and refilled during the evening, adding nectar and seed options. The new hardware did not prompt any visual visits from the two species heard.
